info_hero_sub: A multidrug-resistant yeast of global epidemiological importance — information for medical professionals and the interested public.
info_what_p1: Candida auris is a yeast first isolated in 2009 from the ear canal of a Japanese patient. It is characterized by pronounced resistance to several antifungal classes, high persistence on surfaces, and rapid spread in healthcare facilities.
info_what_p2_pre: In 2022 the WHO classified it as a
info_klinik_a1: Candidemia (bloodstream infection), urinary tract infections, wound infections, and asymptomatic colonization. More rarely meningitis or endocarditis in predisposed patient groups.
info_klinik_a2: Prolonged stays in intensive care units, indwelling catheters (central venous, urinary), prior antifungal therapy, severe underlying conditions (hematological malignancies, diabetes mellitus, renal insufficiency), mechanical ventilation, and prior stays abroad in endemic regions.
info_klinik_a3: Primarily through direct contact — staff hands, contaminated surfaces and devices. Candida auris persists for weeks on inanimate surfaces, even against many standard disinfectants.
info_klinik_a4: Consistent hand hygiene, contact isolation of affected patients, effective surface disinfection with sporicidal agents (e.g. sodium hypochlorite). Alcohol-based disinfectants alone are insufficient.
info_klinik_a5: Standard culture methods may misidentify C. auris. For reliable identification, MALDI-TOF MS (with an up-to-date database) or molecular methods (PCR, ITS sequencing) are recommended. Resistance testing should always be performed.
info_tl_2009_x: Isolate from the ear canal of a Japanese patient — first described by Satoh et al.
info_tl_2012_x: Retrospective analysis reveals earlier cases in South Korea and Pakistan; first clusters in India.
info_tl_2015_x: Included in surveillance by CDC and ECDC. First outbreaks in the United Kingdom.
info_tl_2017_x: Added to the first WHO list of priority fungal pathogens. Detected on all inhabited continents.
info_tl_2022_x: WHO classifies C. auris as a Critical Priority Fungal Pathogen. Accelerated rise post-COVID.
info_tl_2024_x: Rising case numbers in Europe. Clades V and VI newly described. Increasing echinocandin resistance.
info_situation_p1: In Austria, first cases were recorded in the course of the European outbreak. Entries were predominantly from patients with prior stays abroad in high-prevalence regions — particularly South Asia, the Middle East, and Africa.

info_situation_p2_strong: no facility names or patient-related data
info_who_text: All medical facilities with laboratory-confirmed detection of Candida auris — regardless of whether it is a manifest infection or asymptomatic colonization. This includes hospitals, laboratories, nursing homes, and rehabilitation centers.
info_process_title: Step by step — the reporting process
info_proc_1_s: Identification via MALDI-TOF (current database!) or PCR. Perform resistance testing.
info_proc_2_s: The reporting form is publicly accessible, no registration required.
info_proc_3_t: Enter data in a structured way
info_proc_3_s: Details on state, city, infection type, isolation site, travel history, and patient data.
info_proc_4_s: After confirmation, the report is forwarded by email. You receive an acknowledgment of receipt.
info_proc_5_s: The responsible person reviews the details and clarifies any questions if needed.
info_proc_6_s: After validation, the aggregated data appear in the public dashboard at the state level.
info_privacy_p1_post: . They are forwarded by email and only transferred manually after content review.
info_privacy_p2: Only aggregated information at the state level appears in the public dashboard. Facility names or patient-related data are never published.
info_cta_sub: The online form is publicly accessible. Reporting takes about 3–5 minutes.

info_faq_1_q: Is Candida auris dangerous for healthy people?
info_faq_1_a: For healthy individuals with an intact immune system, C. auris generally poses no immediate danger. Severe infections primarily affect immunocompromised or intensive-care patients.
info_faq_2_a: Your report is forwarded by email. After content review, the data are transferred manually. The dashboard shows only aggregated, anonymized information at the state level.
info_faq_3_q: Which disinfectants work against C. auris?
info_faq_3_a: C. auris is tolerant to many standard disinfectants. Chlorine-based agents (sodium hypochlorite) and hydrogen-peroxide-based products are recommended. Alcohol-based agents alone are insufficient.
info_faq_4_q: Do colonization cases also have to be reported?
info_faq_4_a: Yes. Asymptomatic colonization cases should also be reported, as they are relevant for epidemiological surveillance. The infection type is entered in the form as "colonization".
